sections.h2: Which Garrard County office answers which tax question
sections.html:
The PVA owns the value, and the sheriff owns the bill. The PVA neither sets rates nor collects, and the sheriff never assesses property, so an argument over the figure goes to one office and a question about paying goes to the other.

Both sit at 319 Stanford St. in Lancaster. The PVA answers at (859) 792-3291 on weekdays during the 8 to 4 day, and the sheriff's number is (859) 792-3591. Think of the PVA as a state office with a local address. State revenue officials supervise it, and every parcel is valued at full fair cash value as of January 1.

The sheriff collects for 28 taxing districts. They include state and county levies, school districts, and special districts for things like fire protection and libraries. Bills go out on October 1 every year with instructions on due dates, penalties, mortgage-company payment and ways to pay. The County Clerk, at 15 Public Square, Suite 5, records deeds and helps notify and collect on delinquent bills.

sections.h2: Garrard County housing and the local market
sections.html:
Garrard County is in east-central Kentucky, with rolling Bluegrass country over most of it and the Knobs in the southeast corner near Cartersville. Lancaster is the seat and the only city. Lexington is about 28 miles north, and the average commute is 33.1 minutes. All residents were counted as rural in 2020.

  • Population: 18,207 in the 2025 estimate, up 7.4 percent from 2020.
  • Home values: $204,900 is the survey median for 2020 to 2024.
  • Owner-occupied share: 79.9 percent.
  • New-home permits in 2025: 0.
  • Median gross rent: $794. Median household income: $63,087.

The 2020 count showed 7,254 housing units, 9.2 percent of them empty, and 6,584 households. With no permits recorded in 2025, sales are mostly of existing houses and acreage.

sections.h2: Due dates and the early-payment discount
sections.html:
The sheriff expects payment by December 31, and bills leave on October 1, so the early-payment window is about a month long. Under KRS 134.015, paying the entire bill by November 1 trims 2 percent. A January payment costs an extra 5 percent, and later ones cost 10 percent.

When statewide mailing runs late, Revenue can substitute a short calendar: a month with the discount, a month at face, then a month with the 5 percent charge. Whoever held title on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, so an early-year closing needs a clear agreement on the bill.

Unpaid bills change hands on April 15, moving from the sheriff to the County Clerk with a lien recorded on the parcel. Penalties and commissions stack up quickly from there.

How an open Garrard County bill moves through the year
WhenWhat happens to the bill
October 1Sheriff mails the bill
Through November 1Paying in full takes 2 percent off
November 2 to December 31Face amount is due
JanuaryAn extra 5 percent applies
After JanuaryAn extra 10 percent applies
April 15Bill moves to the County Clerk with a recorded lien
Weeks after transferInterest, county attorney letters, then the clerk's sale 90 to 135 days after transfer

Interest is 1 percent per month. A 30-day notice and a second notice come from the county attorney. When a certificate sells to an outside buyer, you owe that buyer plus its additional fees.

Treat the tax bill as part of the sale paperwork. Because the sheriff mails bills in October and the debt belongs to whoever held the property on January 1, a house that closes in spring or summer may still have a bill outstanding in the seller's name.

  • Phone the sheriff's office at (859) 792-3591 for the amount due on the parcel.
  • Ask the County Clerk at (859) 792-3071 how to record the deed, since the clerk's office archives deeds and mortgages.
  • Tell the PVA at (859) 792-3291 who the new owner is so later notices and any exemption follow the right person.
  • Keep the paid receipt with your closing file, because the buyer's title search will otherwise show the balance as open.

An owner behind on taxes and facing repairs on an older farmhouse may also weigh a direct sale to a buyer that closes as-is, which avoids carrying the bill through a long listing. A cash sale skips the lender appraisal and repair requests, and the tax payoff comes out of the proceeds at closing.

Meet with the PVA, then file with the County Clerk. The roll is open for 13 days beginning in early May, and the conference comes first. File by the end of the next business day after viewing closes.

A local board of assessment appeals then meets about four to five weeks later and rules on documented evidence: comparable listings, construction costs, photographs. It must give written reasons for a change. A paid representative must be an attorney, appraiser or another approved professional carrying your written authorization.

Seniors and totally disabled owners can subtract $49,100 from assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Apply at the PVA on Stanford Street.

To show age, bring a birth certificate, license or passport. A seller who has held the exemption should tell the PVA after closing so it ends at that address.

faqs.q: When do Garrard County tax bills go out?
faqs.a: They are mailed on October 1 each year. Payment in full by November 1 earns a 2 percent discount.

faqs.q: Who should I call if a Garrard County tax value looks wrong?
faqs.a: Call the Garrard County PVA at (859) 792-3291. The sheriff's office never assesses value and refers those questions to the PVA.

faqs.q: Where is the Garrard County sheriff's tax office?
faqs.a: It is at 319 Stanford St. in Lancaster, KY 40444, with a phone at (859) 792-3591. The sheriff collects for 28 taxing districts.

faqs.q: What changes for Garrard County taxes still open on April 15?
faqs.a: The bill moves to the County Clerk as a certificate of delinquency with a recorded lien. Interest of 1 percent per month starts, and clerk and attorney commissions follow.

faqs.q: What is the Garrard County homestead exemption worth?
faqs.a: It is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, taken off the assessed value of a home owned by a senior or a totally disabled person.
